decks.title: Similarity — Part 1: Similar figures and the conditions for similar triangles
goals: Tell similar figures from congruent figures using equal angles and proportional sides
Write the correspondence of similar triangles and find the scale factor
Use the AA, SSS and SAS conditions (applied, not proved) to show that triangles are similar
Use similar triangles to find unknown lengths, as in shadow problems

slides.heading: Similarity, Part 1
slides.body_md: Two figures are **similar** when they have the same shape, but not always the same size. In this part we learn to recognise similar triangles and to use them to find lengths.

visual.alt: Two triangles of the same shape. The right-hand triangle PQR is the left-hand triangle ABC enlarged by a factor of three halves. Matching angles carry the same number of arcs: one at A and P, two at B and Q, three at C and R.
visual.caption: Same shape, different size: matching angles equal.

slides.narration: Welcome to similarity. Look at these two triangles. The second is the first one enlarged: the same shape, but a different size. The arcs show that matching angles are equal. In this part we learn how to recognise similar triangles using three simple conditions, and then use them to find unknown lengths.

slides.heading: What you will be able to do
bullets: Write the **correspondence** and find the **scale factor**
Find unknown lengths, for example from **shadows**
slides.narration: These are your goals for part one. First we compare similar and congruent figures. Then we learn to name similar triangles correctly and find the scale factor. Next come the three conditions for similar triangles. We finish by using them to find lengths that we cannot measure directly, such as the height of a tree.

slides.heading: Similar figures: same shape, different size
slides.body_md: Two figures are **similar** when one is an enlargement or a reduction of the other. Matching angles are **equal**, and matching sides are in the **same ratio** $k$, the **scale factor**.
bullets: Here $k = 2$: every side of $\triangle PQR$ is twice the matching side of $\triangle ABC$
enlarging a figure never changes its angles

visual.alt: Triangle ABC with sides 4, 5 and 6 centimetres and triangle PQR with sides 8, 10 and 12 centimetres, drawn to the same scale. Every side of PQR is twice the matching side of ABC, so the scale factor is 2.
visual.caption: Scale factor $k = 2$: $\dfrac{8}{4} = \dfrac{10}{5} = \dfrac{12}{6} = 2$. Lengths in cm.

slides.narration: Similar figures are enlargements or reductions of each other. Their matching angles are equal, and their matching sides are all in the same ratio. That ratio is called the scale factor. Here the second triangle has sides eight, ten and twelve, which are twice four, five and six. So the scale factor is two, and the angles stay the same.

slides.heading: Similar and congruent figures
slides.body_md: Congruent figures are the special case of similar figures with scale factor $k = 1$.

rows: not every similar pair is congruent

visual.alt: Table comparing similar and congruent figures: both have the same shape and equal corresponding angles; similar figures may differ in size and have corresponding sides in the ratio k; congruent figures have the same size, so k equals 1; congruent figures are similar but similar figures need not be congruent.
visual.caption: Congruent means similar with scale factor $1$.

slides.narration: Compare the two ideas. Both kinds of figures have the same shape and equal matching angles. Similar figures may have different sizes, with matching sides in the ratio k. Congruent figures also have the same size, so k equals one. That means every congruent pair is similar, but a similar pair is not always congruent.

slides.heading: Polygons need both tests
slides.body_md: For **triangles**, one test is enough (next slides). For polygons with **four or more sides**, both must hold: equal angles **and** proportional sides.
bullets: a square and a rhombus with equal sides have unequal angles: **not similar**
a $2 \times 3$ rectangle and a $2 \times 5$ rectangle have equal angles but sides in different ratios: **not similar**

visual.alt: A square ABCD and a rhombus PQRS, both with sides 3 centimetres. The square has four right angles; the rhombus has angles of 60 degrees and 120 degrees. Equal sides, but unequal angles, so they are not similar.
visual.caption: Equal sides are not enough: the angles differ ($90^\circ$ against $60^\circ$).

slides.narration: For figures with four or more sides, equal angles alone are not enough, and neither are proportional sides alone. Here a square and a rhombus have equal sides, but the angles are ninety degrees and sixty degrees, so they are not similar. A two by three rectangle and a two by five rectangle have equal angles, but the sides are not in proportion. Triangles are special: one test is enough.

slides.heading: Quick check: guaranteed similar
slides.body_md: Which description leaves nothing free?
slides.narration: Which of these descriptions guarantees that the two figures are similar? Ask whether any angle or any side could still vary.

slides.heading: Naming similar triangles
slides.body_md: Write $\triangle ABC \sim \triangle PQR$ with the vertices in **corresponding order**: $A \to P$, $B \to Q$, $C \to R$. Then angles and sides correspond in that order.

visual.alt: Triangle ABC with BC 4, CA 6 and AB 8 centimetres and triangle PQR with QR 6, RP 9 and PQ 12 centimetres, drawn to scale. Vertices correspond in order: A to P, B to Q, C to R. Matching angles carry the same arcs.
visual.caption: $\triangle ABC \sim \triangle PQR$ with $A \to P$, $B \to Q$, $C \to R$ and $k = \dfrac{3}{2}$. Lengths in cm.

math: \angle A = \angle P, \quad \angle B = \angle Q, \quad \angle C = \angle R
slides.narration: When we write that triangle A B C is similar to triangle P Q R, the order of the letters matters. A matches P, B matches Q and C matches R. So side A B matches side P Q, and the three ratios of matching sides are equal. Here every side of the second triangle is one and a half times the matching side of the first.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: scale factor and missing sides
slides.body_md: $\triangle ABC \sim \triangle PQR$, with $AB = 5$ cm, $BC = 6$ cm, $CA = 7$ cm and $PQ = 7.5$ cm. Find the scale factor, $QR$ and $RP$.

visual.alt: Worked example 1: triangle ABC with BC 6, CA 7 and AB 5 centimetres, and the similar triangle PQR with PQ 7.5 centimetres. The sides QR and RP are to be found.
visual.caption: Given: $AB = 5$, $BC = 6$, $CA = 7$ and $PQ = 7.5$ (cm).

slides.narration: First find the scale factor from the pair of sides we know: seven point five over five is three halves. Then every side of the second triangle is three halves of the matching side. Q R matches B C, so Q R is three halves of six, which is nine. R P matches C A, so R P is three halves of seven, which is ten point five.

slides.heading: Quick check: a missing side
slides.body_md: Match the sides in order, then use the ratio.
slides.narration: Write down which sides correspond, using the order of the letters. Then form the ratio and solve for the missing side.

slides.heading: The AA condition
slides.body_md: If **two angles** of one triangle are equal to **two angles** of another, the triangles are **similar** (the **AA** condition). The third angles are then equal too, because the angles of a triangle add up to $180^\circ$.

visual.alt: Two triangles with two angles marked: 50 degrees at A and 60 degrees at B in triangle ABC, and 50 degrees at P and 60 degrees at Q in triangle PQR. Two equal pairs of angles make the triangles similar, and the third angles are both 70 degrees.
visual.caption: AA: two equal angles. The third angles are $180^\circ - 50^\circ - 60^\circ = 70^\circ$ in both.

math: \angle A = \angle P, \; \angle B = \angle Q \;\Rightarrow\; \triangle ABC \sim \triangle PQR
slides.narration: Here is the first condition, called angle angle. If two angles of one triangle equal two angles of another triangle, the triangles are similar. The third angles must also be equal, because the three angles of any triangle add up to one hundred and eighty degrees. In the picture, fifty and sixty degrees force the third angle to be seventy in both triangles.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: AA gives a length
slides.body_md: In the figure $\angle A = \angle P$ and $\angle B = \angle Q$, with $AB = 6$ cm, $BC = 8$ cm and $PQ = 9$ cm. Find $QR$.
bullets: **Step 1 —** two pairs of equal angles, so $\triangle ABC \sim \triangle PQR$ (AA), with $A \to P$, $B \to Q$, $C \to R$.

visual.alt: Worked example 2: triangles ABC and PQR with the angles at A and P marked equal (one arc) and the angles at B and Q marked equal (two arcs). AB is 6 and BC is 8 centimetres; PQ is 9 centimetres and QR is to be found.
visual.caption: Two equal pairs of angles: $\triangle ABC \sim \triangle PQR$ (AA). Lengths in cm.

slides.narration: Two pairs of equal angles are marked, so the triangles are similar by the angle angle condition. Match the sides in order. Q R over B C equals P Q over A B. So Q R equals nine times eight over six, which is twelve centimetres. Check with the scale factor: it is three halves, and eight times three halves is also twelve.

slides.heading: The SSS condition
slides.body_md: If the **three pairs of sides** of two triangles are in the **same ratio**, the triangles are **similar** (the **SSS** condition). Compare shortest with shortest, and longest with longest.

visual.alt: Triangle ABC with sides 5, 6 and 7 centimetres and triangle PQR with sides 10, 12 and 14 centimetres, drawn to scale. All three pairs of matching sides are in the ratio 1 to 2, so the triangles are similar.
visual.caption: SSS: $\dfrac{5}{10} = \dfrac{6}{12} = \dfrac{7}{14} = \dfrac{1}{2}$. Lengths in cm.

slides.narration: The second condition is called side side side. If all three pairs of matching sides are in the same ratio, the triangles are similar. To compare, put the sides in order of size, shortest with shortest and longest with longest. Here five, six and seven are each half of ten, twelve and fourteen, so the triangles are similar.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: test by SSS
slides.body_md: Are these pairs of triangles similar? (i) sides $6, 8, 12$ and $9, 12, 18$; (ii) sides $4, 5, 7$ and $8, 10, 15$ (all in cm).
bullets: **Step 1 —** order the sides and divide: shortest by shortest, and so on.

visual.alt: Table for worked example 3: the triangles 6, 8, 12 and 9, 12, 18 have all three ratios equal to 2 over 3, so they are similar by the side side side condition; the triangles 4, 5, 7 and 8, 10, 15 have ratios one half, one half and 7 over 15, so they are not similar.
visual.caption: Compare shortest with shortest, longest with longest.

slides.narration: To test by side side side, divide each side of one triangle by the matching side of the other. In the first pair, all three ratios are two thirds, so the triangles are similar. In the second pair, the first two ratios are one half, but the third is seven fifteenths, which is different. One unequal ratio is enough to show the triangles are not similar.

slides.heading: Quick check: which condition?
slides.body_md: Count what is given: angles or sides?
slides.narration: Two pairs of equal angles are given and no side lengths. Which similarity condition does that match?

slides.heading: The SAS condition
slides.body_md: If **one angle** of a triangle equals one angle of another, and the **sides including these angles** are in the same ratio, the triangles are **similar** (the **SAS** condition).
bullets: the angle must lie **between** the two proportional sides

visual.alt: Triangle ABC with AB 3 and BC 5 centimetres around an angle of 120 degrees at B, and triangle PQR with PQ 6 and QR 10 centimetres around an angle of 120 degrees at Q. The sides including the equal angles are in the ratio 1 to 2.
visual.caption: SAS: $\angle B = \angle Q$, $\dfrac{3}{6} = \dfrac{5}{10}$. Lengths in cm.

slides.narration: The third condition is called side angle side. If one angle of a triangle equals one angle of another, and the two sides around that angle are in the same ratio, the triangles are similar. The angle must sit between the two sides. Here both triangles have an angle of one hundred and twenty degrees, and the sides around it are in the ratio one to two.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: SAS and a third side
slides.body_md: $\angle B = \angle Q = 60^\circ$, $AB = 5$ cm, $BC = 8$ cm, $PQ = 7.5$ cm and $QR = 12$ cm. Show that $\triangle ABC \sim \triangle PQR$, and find $PR$ if $AC = 7$ cm.
bullets: **Step 2 —** the included angles are equal, so $\triangle ABC \sim \triangle PQR$ (SAS).

visual.alt: Worked example 4: triangle ABC with AB 5, BC 8 and AC 7 centimetres and an angle of 60 degrees at B, and triangle PQR with PQ 7.5, QR 12 centimetres and an angle of 60 degrees at Q. PR is to be found.
visual.caption: Equal included angles and $\dfrac{5}{7.5} = \dfrac{8}{12}$: SAS. Lengths in cm.

slides.narration: Divide the sides around the equal angle. Five over seven point five is two thirds, and eight over twelve is also two thirds. The angle between them is equal in both triangles, so the triangles are similar by side angle side. The third sides are then in the same ratio, so P R is seven times three over two, which is ten point five centimetres.

slides.heading: Which condition should I use?
slides.body_md: Look at what is **given**, then pick the condition that needs exactly those facts. You **use** the conditions in this syllabus; you do not have to prove them.

nodes.label: Compare two triangles: which facts are given?
Two pairs of equal angles: use AA
Three pairs of sides in the same ratio: use SSS
One equal angle between two proportional pairs of sides: use SAS

visual.alt: Flow chart for choosing a similarity condition: start from the facts given about two triangles; if two pairs of angles are equal use the angle angle condition; if three pairs of sides are in the same ratio use the side side side condition; if one angle is equal and the sides around it are in the same ratio use the side angle side condition.
visual.caption: Match the facts to the condition. No need to prove the conditions: just use them.

slides.narration: To choose a condition, look at what you are given. Two pairs of equal angles point to angle angle. Three pairs of sides in the same ratio point to side side side. One equal angle between two proportional pairs of sides points to side angle side. The syllabus asks you to use these conditions, not to prove them.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: the height of a tree
slides.body_md: A stick $1.2$ m long casts a shadow $1.6$ m long. At the same moment a tree casts a shadow $12$ m long. How tall is the tree?
bullets: **Step 1 —** the sun's rays are parallel and the stick and tree are vertical, so the right triangles are similar (AA).
**Check —** the tree is $9$ m high and its shadow is $12$ m: $\dfrac{9}{12} = \dfrac{3}{4}$, the same as $\dfrac{1.2}{1.6}$.

visual.alt: A stick 1.2 metres tall with a shadow of 1.6 metres, and a tree beside it with a shadow of 12 metres in the same sunlight. The two right triangles share the same sun angle, so they are similar.
visual.caption: Stick $AB$ and tree $PQ$; shadows $AC$ and $PR$. Lengths in m.

slides.narration: The sun shines at the same angle on the stick and on the tree, and both stand straight up. So the two right triangles have two equal angles and are similar. The height of the tree over its shadow equals the height of the stick over its shadow. That gives twelve times one point two over one point six, which is nine metres.

slides.heading: Worked example 6: triangles sharing an angle
slides.body_md: In $\triangle ABC$, $AB = 12$ cm, $AC = 8$ cm, $BC = 10$ cm. $D$ is on $AB$ with $AD = 3$ cm, and $E$ is on $AC$ with $\angle ADE = \angle ACB$. Find $AE$ and $DE$.
bullets: **Step 1 —** $\angle A$ is common and $\angle ADE = \angle ACB$: $\triangle ADE \sim \triangle ACB$ (AA), with $D \to C$, $E \to B$.

visual.alt: Worked example 6: triangle ABC with AB 12, AC 8 and BC 10 centimetres. D is on AB with AD 3 centimetres, and E is on AC so that the angle at D in triangle ADE equals the angle at C in triangle ABC, shown by single arcs.
visual.caption: Angle $A$ is common and $\angle ADE = \angle ACB$: $\triangle ADE \sim \triangle ACB$. Lengths in cm.

slides.narration: The two triangles share the angle at A, and the angle at D equals the angle at C. That is two equal angles, so they are similar. Careful with the order: D matches C and E matches B. Then A E over A B equals A D over A C, which gives A E equal to four point five. And D E over C B equals A D over A C, which gives D E equal to three point seven five.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Similar: equal matching angles, matching sides in the ratio $k$
AA, SSS and SAS prove triangles similar
Shadows: parallel rays make similar right triangles

rows: three pairs of sides in one ratio
an equal angle between two proportional pairs of sides
matching sides in the ratio $k$; matching angles equal

visual.alt: Summary table of the three conditions for similar triangles: AA needs two pairs of equal angles; SSS needs three pairs of sides in one ratio; SAS needs an equal angle between two proportional pairs of sides; the result is that matching sides are in the ratio k and matching angles are equal.
visual.caption: Part 1 on one card.

slides.narration: To sum up part one. Similar figures have equal matching angles and matching sides in one ratio. Congruent figures are the case where that ratio is one. Always write similar triangles in corresponding order. The conditions angle angle, side side side and side angle side prove triangles similar, and shadow problems are a classic use of them.

slides.heading: Exam tips: how marks are awarded
bullets: **State the condition (1 mark):** name AA, SSS or SAS and give the equal angles or ratios
**Correspondence (1 mark):** write $\triangle ABC \sim \triangle PQR$ in matching order
**Proportion and answer (1–2 marks):** substitute, then solve
**Mistake:** matching the wrong sides when the letters are in a different order
**Mistake:** using SAS when the angle is **not** between the two proportional sides
**Habit:** check that the larger triangle has the larger sides
slides.narration: In the exam, name the condition and give the facts that justify it. Write the similarity in corresponding order, because that is where the marks for matching sides come from. Then write the proportion and solve it. Watch two common slips: matching the wrong sides, and using side angle side when the angle is not between the two sides.

decks.title: Similarity — Part 2: Proportionality, areas, maps and models
goals: Use the Basic Proportionality Theorem and its converse to find lengths and test for parallel lines
Use similar triangles in a trapezium with its diagonals
Find the ratio of areas of similar triangles from the ratio of sides, and the reverse
Use a scale factor to convert lengths, areas and volumes between a map or model and the real object

slides.heading: Similarity, Part 2
slides.body_md: A line drawn **parallel to one side** of a triangle cuts the other two sides **in the same ratio**. This gives a powerful way to find lengths, and, with areas, scale factors and models, a way to compare sizes.

visual.alt: Triangle ABC with a line DE parallel to the base BC. D is on AB and E is on AC and they divide the two sides in the same ratio, 2 to 3.
visual.caption: A line parallel to one side cuts the other two sides in the same ratio.

slides.narration: Welcome to part two. This line is parallel to the base of the triangle, and look how it cuts the two sloping sides in the same ratio. This is the basic proportionality theorem. In this part we use it to find lengths, then move on to areas of similar triangles, and finally to maps and scale models.

slides.heading: What you will be able to do
bullets: Use the **Basic Proportionality Theorem** and its **converse**
Use similar triangles in a **trapezium** with its diagonals
Convert **lengths, areas and volumes** on maps and models
slides.narration: These are your goals for part two. We use the basic proportionality theorem and its converse. We use similar triangles inside a trapezium. We learn that areas of similar triangles go as the square of the sides. And we finish with maps and models, where lengths, areas and volumes scale differently.

slides.heading: The Basic Proportionality Theorem
slides.body_md: If a line is drawn **parallel to one side** of a triangle, it divides the other two sides **in the same ratio**.
bullets: it is used, not proved, in this syllabus

visual.alt: Triangle ABC with DE parallel to BC. AD and DB are the parts of side AB; AE and EC are the parts of side AC. The theorem says that AD over DB equals AE over EC.
visual.caption: Basic Proportionality Theorem: $DE \parallel BC \Rightarrow \dfrac{AD}{DB} = \dfrac{AE}{EC}$.

slides.narration: Here is the basic proportionality theorem. If a line D E is parallel to the side B C of a triangle A B C, then it divides the sides A B and A C in the same ratio. A D over D B equals A E over E C. We use this theorem directly, without needing to prove it.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: finding a length
slides.body_md: In $\triangle ABC$, $DE \parallel BC$, $AD = 3$ cm, $DB = 4.5$ cm and $AE = 2.4$ cm. Find $EC$ and $AC$.

visual.alt: Worked example 1: triangle ABC with DE parallel to BC. AD is 3, DB is 4.5 and AE is 2.4 centimetres; EC is to be found.
visual.caption: Given $AD = 3$, $DB = 4.5$, $AE = 2.4$ (cm).

slides.narration: Write the proportion: A D over D B equals A E over E C. Put in the numbers: three over four point five equals two point four over E C. Solving gives E C equal to two point four times four point five over three, which is three point six centimetres. The whole side A C is two point four plus three point six, which is six centimetres.

slides.heading: Equivalent forms of the theorem
slides.body_md: Because $\triangle ADE \sim \triangle ABC$, the theorem can be written in several equivalent ways. Choose the one that has your unknown in it.

rows: add $1$ to both sides, or use $\triangle ADE \sim \triangle ABC$

visual.alt: Table of equivalent forms of the Basic Proportionality Theorem: AD over DB equals AE over EC; AD over AB equals AE over AC; with the parallel line DE over BC added; and DB over AB equals EC over AC.
visual.caption: Four ways to write the same fact.

slides.narration: The theorem can be written in four equivalent ways. We can compare the two parts on each side. We can compare a part to the whole side. Adding the parallel line gives three equal ratios, because the small triangle is similar to the whole triangle. And we can compare the lower parts to the whole sides. Pick the form that contains your unknown.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: an unknown in the proportion
slides.body_md: In $\triangle ABC$, $DE \parallel BC$, $AD = x$, $DB = 6$, $AE = x + 2$ and $EC = 9$ (cm). Find $x$.

visual.alt: Worked example 2: triangle ABC with DE parallel to BC. AD is x, DB is 6, AE is x plus 2 and EC is 9 centimetres.
visual.caption: Unknown $x$ in the proportion. Lengths in cm.

slides.narration: Write the proportion with x in it: x over six equals x plus two over nine. Cross multiply: nine x equals six x plus twelve. Collect the terms: three x equals twelve, so x is four. Check: four over six and six over nine are both two thirds, so the proportion holds.

slides.heading: The converse
slides.body_md: If a line divides **two sides** of a triangle **in the same ratio**, then it is **parallel to the third side**.
bullets: use it to **prove** that two lines are parallel
the ratios must be taken in the **same order** on both sides

visual.alt: Triangle ABC with D on AB and E on AC dividing both sides in the ratio 2 to 3. By the converse of the theorem, DE is parallel to BC.
visual.caption: Converse: equal ratios on the two sides $\Rightarrow$ $DE \parallel BC$.

slides.narration: The converse of the theorem works the other way. If a line cuts two sides of a triangle in the same ratio, then it is parallel to the third side. We use this to show that two lines are parallel. Take care to write both ratios in the same order, upper part first on both sides.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: is DE parallel to BC?
slides.body_md: $D$ is on $AB$ and $E$ is on $AC$ with $AD = 5$, $DB = 7.5$, $AE = 4$, $EC = 6$ (cm). Is $DE \parallel BC$? What if $EC$ were $5$ cm?
bullets: **Step 2 —** the ratios are equal, so $DE \parallel BC$ by the converse.
**Step 3 —** with $EC = 5$: $\dfrac{4}{5} \ne \dfrac{2}{3}$, so $DE$ would not be parallel to $BC$.

visual.alt: Worked example 3: triangle ABC with D on AB and E on AC. AD is 5 and DB is 7.5 centimetres; AE is 4 and EC is 6 centimetres. The two ratios are both 2 to 3.
visual.caption: If $\dfrac{AD}{DB} = \dfrac{AE}{EC}$ then $DE \parallel BC$. Lengths in cm.

slides.narration: Compare the two ratios in the same order. Five over seven point five is two thirds. Four over six is also two thirds. They are equal, so D E is parallel to B C by the converse theorem. If E C were five instead, four over five would not equal two thirds, so D E would not be parallel to B C.

slides.heading: Quick check: which set gives parallel lines?
slides.body_md: Compare the two ratios in the same order.
slides.narration: For each set of lengths, work out the ratio on one side and the ratio on the other side, upper part first. Only one set gives equal ratios.

slides.heading: Diagonals of a trapezium
slides.body_md: In trapezium $ABCD$ with $AB \parallel DC$, the diagonals meet at $O$. Triangles $AOB$ and $COD$ are **similar** (AA: vertically opposite angles, alternate angles).

visual.alt: Trapezium ABCD with AB 12 centimetres at the bottom and DC 8 centimetres on top, parallel to it. The diagonals AC and BD cross at O, forming triangles AOB and COD.
visual.caption: Triangles $AOB$ and $COD$ are similar (AA): $\dfrac{AO}{OC} = \dfrac{BO}{OD} = \dfrac{AB}{DC} = \dfrac{3}{2}$. Lengths in cm.

slides.narration: In a trapezium with A B parallel to D C, the diagonals cross at a point O. Look at triangles A O B and C O D. The angles at O are vertically opposite, and the other angles are alternate angles between the parallel sides. So the triangles are similar, and the diagonals are cut in the same ratio as the parallel sides. Here that ratio is three to two.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: a trapezium
slides.body_md: In trapezium $ABCD$, $AB \parallel DC$, $AB = 15$ cm, $DC = 9$ cm, and the diagonals meet at $O$ with $AO = 10$ cm. Find $OC$ and the ratio $BO : OD$.

visual.alt: Worked example 4: trapezium ABCD with AB 15 centimetres parallel to DC 9 centimetres. The diagonals meet at O and AO is 10 centimetres; OC is to be found.
visual.caption: Given $AB = 15$, $DC = 9$, $AO = 10$ (cm).

slides.narration: The triangles A O B and C O D are similar, so A O over O C equals A B over D C, which is fifteen over nine, or five thirds. Then O C is ten times nine over fifteen, which is six centimetres. The other diagonal is cut in the same ratio, so B O to O D is five to three.

slides.heading: Areas of similar triangles
slides.body_md: The areas of two similar triangles are in the ratio of the **squares** of their corresponding sides.
bullets: the same ratio holds for corresponding **altitudes** and **medians**, and the perimeters follow the sides

visual.alt: Triangle ABC with sides 3, 4 and 5 centimetres, area 6 square centimetres, and its enlargement PQR with sides 6, 8 and 10 centimetres, area 24 square centimetres. The sides are doubled and the area is multiplied by four.
visual.caption: Sides $\times 2$, area $\times 4$: $6 \to 24$ cm$^2$.

slides.narration: Here is a key fact about areas. When two triangles are similar, the ratio of their areas is the square of the ratio of corresponding sides. In this picture the sides are doubled, so the area is multiplied by four: from six square centimetres to twenty four. Altitudes and medians scale like sides, and so do perimeters.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: the ratio of areas
slides.body_md: Corresponding sides of two similar triangles are $6$ cm and $10$ cm. Find the ratio of their areas. If the larger area is $75$ cm$^2$, find the smaller.

visual.alt: Table for worked example 5: the ratio of corresponding sides 6 to 10 is 3 to 5; the ratio of areas is 3 over 5 squared, which is 9 over 25; the smaller area is 9 over 25 of 75, which is 27 square centimetres.
visual.caption: Square the ratio of sides to get the ratio of areas.

slides.narration: The ratio of the sides is six to ten, which simplifies to three to five. Square it: the ratio of areas is nine to twenty five. The smaller triangle has nine twenty fifths of the larger area. Nine twenty fifths of seventy five square centimetres is twenty seven square centimetres.

slides.heading: Worked example 6: from areas to sides
slides.body_md: Two similar triangles have areas $20$ cm$^2$ and $45$ cm$^2$. A side of the smaller is $8$ cm. Find the corresponding side of the larger.
bullets: **Step 2 —** ratio of sides is the square root: $\sqrt{\dfrac{4}{9}} = \dfrac{2}{3}$.

rows: Corresponding side of the larger triangle

visual.alt: Table for worked example 6: the ratio of areas 20 to 45 is 4 to 9; the ratio of sides is its square root, 2 to 3; the corresponding side of the larger triangle is 8 times 3 over 2, which is 12 centimetres.
visual.caption: Square root of the area ratio gives the side ratio.

slides.narration: Now we go the other way. The ratio of areas is twenty to forty five, which is four ninths. The ratio of sides is the square root of that, two thirds. So the larger triangle has sides three halves as long. Eight times three halves is twelve centimetres.

slides.heading: Worked example 7: a parallel line and areas
slides.body_md: $DE \parallel BC$ in $\triangle ABC$, with $AD : DB = 3 : 2$, $BC = 20$ cm and area $\triangle ABC = 100$ cm$^2$. Find $DE$, the area of $\triangle ADE$ and the area of trapezium $DBCE$.

The area of A D E is three fifths squared times one hundred, which is thirty six. The trapezium is what is left: one hundred minus thirty six, which is sixty four square centimetres.

slides.heading: Scale and maps
slides.body_md: A map or model drawn to scale $1 : n$ has every **length** $n$ times smaller than the real length: map length $= \dfrac{\text{real length}}{n}$. **Areas** shrink by $n^2$.
bullets: change units at the end: $100\,000$ cm $= 1$ km

Areas shrink by the square of n, so one square centimetre on that map stands for a quarter of a square kilometre. Remember to change centimetres to kilometres at the end.

slides.body_md: A map has scale $1 : 30\,000$. (i) A path measures $6.5$ cm on the map: real length? (ii) A lake covers $8$ cm$^2$: real area? (iii) A road is $4.5$ km long: length on the map?

slides.heading: Lengths, areas and volumes
slides.body_md: If a model has scale factor $k$ (model : real), then **lengths** are in the ratio $k$, **areas** in the ratio $k^2$ and **volumes** in the ratio $k^3$.

A model at one to twenty has one four hundredth of the area and one eight thousandth of the volume of the real object. This is why a small model holds much less than a small fraction of the real thing.

sections.heading: 1. Similar figures and scale factor
sections.body_md:
- Two figures are **similar** when they have the same shape: corresponding angles are **equal** and corresponding sides are in the **same ratio** $k$ (the **scale factor**).
- An enlargement ($k > 1$) or a reduction ($k < 1$) keeps all angles.
- **Congruent** figures are similar with $k = 1$.
- For triangles, one test is enough (see section 3). For polygons with four or more sides, **both** equal angles **and** proportional sides are needed: a square and a rhombus of equal sides are not similar.

*Example:* triangles with sides $4, 5, 6$ and $8, 10, 12$ cm are similar with $k = 2$.

key_terms.definition_md: Figures of the same shape: equal corresponding angles, corresponding sides in a constant ratio.
The constant ratio $k$ of corresponding sides.

visual.alt: Triangle ABC with sides 4, 5 and 6 centimetres and triangle PQR with sides 8, 10 and 12 centimetres, drawn to the same scale. Every side of PQR is twice the matching side of ABC, so the scale factor is 2.
visual.caption: Scale factor $k = 2$: $\dfrac{8}{4} = \dfrac{10}{5} = \dfrac{12}{6} = 2$. Lengths in cm.

visuals.alt: A square ABCD and a rhombus PQRS, both with sides 3 centimetres. The square has four right angles; the rhombus has angles of 60 degrees and 120 degrees. Equal sides, but unequal angles, so they are not similar.
visuals.caption: Equal sides are not enough: the angles differ ($90^\circ$ against $60^\circ$).

sections.heading: 2. Similar and congruent; naming in order
sections.body_md:
- Similar: same shape, size may differ. Congruent: same shape **and** size.
- Every congruent pair is similar ($k = 1$); not every similar pair is congruent.
- Write $\triangle ABC \sim \triangle PQR$ with vertices in **corresponding order**: $A \to P$, $B \to Q$, $C \to R$. Then $\angle A = \angle P$ and so on, and $\dfrac{AB}{PQ} = \dfrac{BC}{QR} = \dfrac{CA}{RP}$.

*Example:* $\triangle ABC \sim \triangle PQR$, $AB = 5$, $BC = 6$, $CA = 7$ cm, $PQ = 7.5$ cm: $k = \dfrac{7.5}{5} = \dfrac{3}{2}$, $QR = 9$ cm, $RP = 10.5$ cm.

key_terms.definition_md: Writing the vertices of similar triangles so that the first letters match, the second letters match and the third letters match.

rows: not every similar pair is congruent

sections.heading: 3. Conditions for similar triangles: AA, SSS, SAS
sections.body_md:
- **AA:** two pairs of equal angles. The third angles are then equal.
- **SSS:** three pairs of sides in the same ratio (compare shortest with shortest).
- **SAS:** one equal angle, and the two sides **including** it in the same ratio.
- These conditions are **used**, not proved, in the ICSE 2027 syllabus.

*Example:* $6, 8, 12$ and $9, 12, 18$ cm: ratios $\dfrac{2}{3}, \dfrac{2}{3}, \dfrac{2}{3}$, so similar (SSS). $4, 5, 7$ and $8, 10, 15$: $\dfrac{1}{2}, \dfrac{1}{2}, \dfrac{7}{15}$, so not similar.

key_terms.definition_md: Two pairs of equal angles make two triangles similar.
Three pairs of sides in the same ratio make two triangles similar.
An equal angle between two proportional pairs of sides makes two triangles similar.

rows: three pairs of sides in one ratio
an equal angle between two proportional pairs of sides

sections.heading: 4. Using similar triangles
sections.body_md:
- Name the similar triangles, **state the condition**, write the proportion in matching order, then solve.
- **Shadows:** the sun's rays are parallel and objects are vertical, so the triangles are similar (AA): $\dfrac{\text{height}}{\text{shadow}}$ is the same for both.
- **Common angle:** if $\angle A$ is shared and $\angle ADE = \angle ACB$, then $\triangle ADE \sim \triangle ACB$ with $D \to C$ and $E \to B$.
- **Right angle:** a perpendicular from the right angle to the hypotenuse splits the triangle into two triangles similar to it (AA).

*Example:* a $1.2$ m stick has a $1.6$ m shadow; a tree's shadow is $12$ m, so the tree is $\dfrac{12 \times 1.2}{1.6} = 9$ m high.

sections.heading: 5. Basic Proportionality Theorem and its converse
sections.body_md:
- **Theorem:** a line parallel to one side of a triangle divides the other two sides in the same ratio: $DE \parallel BC \Rightarrow \dfrac{AD}{DB} = \dfrac{AE}{EC}$. Equivalent forms: $\dfrac{AD}{AB} = \dfrac{AE}{AC} = \dfrac{DE}{BC}$.
- **Converse:** if $\dfrac{AD}{DB} = \dfrac{AE}{EC}$ (same order), then $DE \parallel BC$.
- **Trapezium:** in $ABCD$ with $AB \parallel DC$, diagonals meet at $O$: $\triangle AOB \sim \triangle COD$ and $\dfrac{AO}{OC} = \dfrac{BO}{OD} = \dfrac{AB}{DC}$.

*Example:* $AD = 3$, $DB = 4.5$, $AE = 2.4$ cm: $EC = \dfrac{2.4 \times 4.5}{3} = 3.6$ cm. With $AD = 5$, $DB = 7.5$, $AE = 4$, $EC = 6$ both ratios are $\dfrac{2}{3}$, so $DE \parallel BC$.

key_terms.definition_md: A line parallel to one side of a triangle cuts the other two sides in the same ratio.
If a line cuts two sides in the same ratio, it is parallel to the third side.

sections.heading: 6. Areas of similar triangles
sections.body_md:
- The areas of similar triangles are in the ratio of the **squares** of corresponding sides: $\dfrac{\text{area}_1}{\text{area}_2} = \left(\dfrac{a_1}{a_2}\right)^2$.
- The same ratio holds for the squares of corresponding altitudes and medians; **perimeters** follow the sides (not squared).
- To go from areas to sides, take the **square root**.
- For $DE \parallel BC$: $\triangle ADE \sim \triangle ABC$, so $\dfrac{\text{area } ADE}{\text{area } ABC} = \left(\dfrac{AD}{AB}\right)^2$, and the trapezium $DBCE$ is the difference.

*Example:* sides $6 : 10$, larger area $75$: smaller $= \dfrac{9}{25} \times 75 = 27$. Areas $20 : 45$, side $8$: larger side $= 8 \times \dfrac{3}{2} = 12$.

key_terms.definition_md: For similar triangles, the square of the ratio of corresponding sides.

sections.heading: 7. Maps and models
sections.body_md:
- A scale $1 : n$ means **lengths** on the map or model are $\dfrac{1}{n}$ of the real lengths; **areas** are $\dfrac{1}{n^2}$; **volumes** are $\dfrac{1}{n^3}$.
- With scale factor $k$ (model : real): lengths $k$, areas $k^2$, volumes $k^3$.
- Convert units at the end: $1$ km $= 100\,000$ cm, $1$ m$^2 = 10\,000$ cm$^2$, $1$ m$^3 = 1\,000\,000$ cm$^3$.
- Going from real to map divides by $n$ (lengths), $n^2$ (areas), $n^3$ (volumes); going from map to real multiplies.

*Example:* on a $1 : 30\,000$ map, $6.5$ cm is $1.95$ km and $8$ cm$^2$ is $0.72$ km$^2$. A $1 : 50$ model of a $125$ m$^3$ tank holds $1000$ cm$^3$.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**How marks are awarded**
- *Similar triangles (2–3 marks):* state the condition with the equal angles or ratios 1; correspondence in order 1; proportion and answer 1.
- *Basic Proportionality Theorem (2–3 marks):* quote the theorem or the similar triangles 1; proportion 1; answer 1.
- *Ratio of areas (2–3 marks):* ratio of sides 1; squared 1; answer 1.
- *Maps and models (2–4 marks):* scale factor for length 1; squared or cubed for area or volume 1–2; units 1.
- *10-mark structured question:* parts (a), (b), (c), usually $3 + 3 + 4$; show every ratio and substitution.

**Common mistakes**
1. Matching sides in the wrong order because the vertices are not written in corresponding order.
2. Using SAS when the equal angle is not between the two proportional sides.
3. Using the ratio of sides as the ratio of areas (areas need the square) or as the ratio of volumes (volumes need the cube).
4. Writing the ratios in a different order on the two sides when using the converse of the theorem.
5. Dividing a map area by $n$ instead of $n^2$, or forgetting to change cm to km.
6. Taking the ratio of areas instead of its square root when finding a side.

cards.front_md: What makes two figures **similar**?
cards.back_md: Equal corresponding angles and corresponding sides in the same ratio $k$ (the scale factor).

cards.front_md: How are congruent figures related to similar figures?
cards.back_md: Congruent figures are similar with scale factor $k = 1$.

cards.front_md: Are a square and a rhombus of equal sides similar?
cards.back_md: No: the sides are proportional but the angles differ ($90^\circ$ against, say, $60^\circ$).

cards.front_md: For triangles, how many tests are needed for similarity?
cards.back_md: One of AA, SSS or SAS is enough; for polygons with four or more sides both equal angles and proportional sides are needed.

cards.front_md: What does $\triangle ABC \sim \triangle PQR$ tell you about the vertices?
cards.back_md: They correspond in order: $A \to P$, $B \to Q$, $C \to R$.

cards.front_md: Scale factor when $AB = 5$ cm corresponds to $PQ = 7.5$ cm?
State the **AA** condition.
cards.back_md: Two pairs of equal angles make two triangles similar; the third angles are then equal too.

cards.front_md: State the **SSS** condition.
cards.back_md: Three pairs of corresponding sides in the same ratio make two triangles similar.

cards.front_md: State the **SAS** condition.
cards.back_md: One equal angle and the sides including it in the same ratio make two triangles similar.

cards.front_md: Are $4, 5, 7$ and $8, 10, 15$ cm triangles similar?
cards.back_md: $\dfrac{4}{8} = \dfrac{5}{10} = \dfrac{1}{2}$ but $\dfrac{7}{15} \ne \dfrac{1}{2}$: not similar.

cards.front_md: Which condition needs no side lengths?
cards.back_md: AA: only two pairs of equal angles.

cards.front_md: Common slip with SAS?
cards.back_md: Using an angle that is **not** between the two proportional sides.

cards.front_md: Why are the triangles formed by a stick and a tree, with their shadows, similar?
cards.back_md: The sun's rays are parallel and both objects are vertical: two equal angles, so AA.

cards.front_md: A $1.2$ m stick has a $1.6$ m shadow. Height of a tree with a $12$ m shadow?
State the **Basic Proportionality Theorem**.
cards.back_md: A line parallel to one side of a triangle divides the other two sides in the same ratio: $DE \parallel BC \Rightarrow \dfrac{AD}{DB} = \dfrac{AE}{EC}$.

cards.front_md: State its **converse**.
cards.back_md: If a line divides two sides in the same ratio, it is parallel to the third side.

cards.front_md: Other forms of the theorem, using the whole side?

questions.stem_md: What must be true of every pair of similar polygons, such as a photograph and its enlargement?

options.text_md: Corresponding angles are equal and corresponding sides are in the same ratio.
Corresponding sides are equal and corresponding angles are in the same ratio.
The two polygons have equal areas.
The two polygons have equal perimeters.

questions.solution_md: Similar figures have the same shape: every pair of corresponding angles is equal and every pair of corresponding sides is in one constant ratio, the scale factor. Their areas and perimeters are equal only when the scale factor is $1$, that is, when the figures are congruent.

questions.stem_md: A triangular kite with sides $14$ cm, $21$ cm and $28$ cm is similar to a smaller one with sides $10$ cm, $15$ cm and $20$ cm. The sides of the larger kite are to the corresponding sides of the smaller kite in the ratio
questions.solution_md: Divide each side of the larger kite by the corresponding side of the smaller: $\dfrac{14}{10} = \dfrac{7}{5}$, $\dfrac{21}{15} = \dfrac{7}{5}$, $\dfrac{28}{20} = \dfrac{7}{5}$. The ratio is $7 : 5$. Option (c) is the ratio the other way round, (d) is the ratio of areas and (a) compares $14$ with the longest side $20$, which is not its corresponding side.

questions.stem_md: Four descriptions of two figures are given. Which one guarantees that the two figures are similar?

options.text_md: two rhombuses, with sides $5$ cm and $10$ cm
two isosceles triangles, with bases $4$ cm and $8$ cm
two squares, one of side $4$ cm and one of side $9$ cm
two rectangles, with lengths $6$ cm and $9$ cm

questions.solution_md: Squares have all angles $90^\circ$ and all sides in the ratio $4 : 9$, so they are always similar. The other three descriptions leave something free: the breadths of the rectangles, the angles of the rhombuses and the equal sides of the isosceles triangles, so the figures need not be similar.

questions.stem_md: In $\triangle ABC$ and $\triangle PQR$, $\angle A = \angle P = 48^\circ$ and $\angle B = \angle Q = 77^\circ$. Which condition proves $\triangle ABC \sim \triangle PQR$?

options.text_md: SSS: three pairs of proportional sides
SAS: an equal angle between proportional sides
RHS: a right angle, hypotenuse and a side
AA: two pairs of equal angles

questions.solution_md: Two pairs of angles are equal, which is the AA condition. The third angles are then equal too: $180^\circ - 48^\circ - 77^\circ = 55^\circ$ in each triangle. No side lengths are given, so SSS and SAS cannot be used, and there is no right angle.

questions.stem_md: If $\triangle DEF \sim \triangle XYZ$, written in this order of vertices, then $\dfrac{EF}{YZ}$ is equal to

options.text_md: $\dfrac{DE}{XY}$
$\dfrac{DE}{XZ}$
$\dfrac{DF}{XY}$
$\dfrac{EF}{XZ}$

questions.solution_md: The order of letters gives the correspondence $D \to X$, $E \to Y$, $F \to Z$. So $EF$ corresponds to $YZ$, $DE$ to $XY$ and $DF$ to $XZ$, and $\dfrac{EF}{YZ} = \dfrac{DE}{XY} = \dfrac{DF}{XZ}$. The other options pair sides that do not correspond.

questions.stem_md: $\triangle LMN \sim \triangle XYZ$ with $LM = 9$ cm, $XY = 6$ cm and $MN = 15$ cm. The length of $YZ$, in cm, is
questions.solution_md: $LM$ and $MN$ correspond to $XY$ and $YZ$. With $YZ = x$ cm: $\dfrac{9}{6} = \dfrac{15}{x} \Rightarrow x = \dfrac{15 \times 6}{9} = 10$. Option (c) turns the ratio upside down, and (d) subtracts the difference $9 - 6$ from $15$.

questions.stem_md: In $\triangle ABC$ and $\triangle DEF$, $\angle A = \angle D = 64^\circ$, $AB = 6$ cm, $AC = 9$ cm, $DE = 8$ cm and $DF = 12$ cm. Which statement is correct?

options.text_md: $\triangle ABC \sim \triangle DEF$ by the AA condition
The two triangles need not be similar
$\triangle ABC \sim \triangle DEF$ by the SAS condition
$\triangle ABC \sim \triangle DEF$ by the SSS condition

questions.solution_md: The sides that include the equal angles are proportional: $\dfrac{AB}{DE} = \dfrac{6}{8} = \dfrac{3}{4}$ and $\dfrac{AC}{DF} = \dfrac{9}{12} = \dfrac{3}{4}$. One angle equal and its including sides proportional is the SAS condition. SSS would need the third pair of sides and AA a second pair of angles; neither is given.

questions.stem_md: A straight cut $DE$ parallel to the base $BC$ of a triangular sail $ABC$ meets $AB$ at $D$ and $AC$ at $E$. Given $AD = 4$ cm, $DB = 6$ cm and $AE = 6$ cm, what is $EC$, in cm?
questions.solution_md: By the Basic Proportionality Theorem, $\dfrac{AD}{DB} = \dfrac{AE}{EC}$, so $EC = \dfrac{AE \times DB}{AD} = \dfrac{6 \times 6}{4} = 9$ cm. Option (a) uses $\dfrac{AD}{DB}$ upside down, and (b) adds the difference $6 - 4$ to $6$.

questions.stem_md: In $\triangle ABC$, a line parallel to $BC$ cuts $AB$ at $D$ and $AC$ at $E$, with $AD = x$, $DB = x - 3$, $AE = x + 2$ and $EC = x - 2$ (all in cm). The value of $x$ is
questions.solution_md: The Basic Proportionality Theorem gives $\dfrac{x}{x - 3} = \dfrac{x + 2}{x - 2}$, that is $x(x - 2) = (x - 3)(x + 2)$: $x(x - 2) = (x - 3)(x + 2) \Rightarrow x^2 - 2x = x^2 - x - 6 \Rightarrow x = 6$. Check: $AD = 6$, $DB = 3$, $AE = 8$, $EC = 4$, and $\dfrac{6}{3} = \dfrac{8}{4}$. Option (b) is $DB$ and (c) is $AE$.

questions.stem_md: $M$ lies on side $PQ$ and $N$ on side $PR$ of $\triangle PQR$. For which set of lengths (in cm) can we be sure that $MN \parallel QR$?
questions.solution_md: By the converse of the Basic Proportionality Theorem, $MN \parallel QR$ exactly when $\dfrac{PM}{MQ} = \dfrac{PN}{NR}$. In (b): $\dfrac{6}{9} = \dfrac{2}{3}$ and $\dfrac{8}{12} = \dfrac{2}{3}$, which are equal. The other sets give $\dfrac{2}{3}$ against $\dfrac{4}{5}$, $\dfrac{3}{2}$ against $\dfrac{9}{8}$, and $\dfrac{5}{7}$ against $\dfrac{7}{5}$.

questions.stem_md: In trapezium $PQRS$, $PQ \parallel SR$ with $PQ = 16$ cm and $SR = 12$ cm. The diagonals $PR$ and $QS$ meet at $T$, and $PT = 8$ cm. How long is $TR$, in cm?
questions.solution_md: $\triangle PTQ \sim \triangle RTS$ (AA), so $\dfrac{PT}{TR} = \dfrac{PQ}{SR} = \dfrac{16}{12}$, and $TR = \dfrac{8 \times 12}{16} = 6$ cm. Option (d) uses the ratio the wrong way up, (a) subtracts $16 - 12$ from $8$ and (b) assumes the diagonals bisect each other.

questions.stem_md: Two triangular flags are similar, and their corresponding sides are in the ratio $4 : 7$. In what ratio are their areas?
questions.solution_md: The areas of similar triangles are in the ratio of the squares of corresponding sides: $\left(\dfrac{4}{7}\right)^2 = \dfrac{16}{49}$. Option (a) is the ratio of the sides, (b) is the ratio of volumes of similar solids and (c) is $16 : 49$ turned upside down.

questions.stem_md: Two similar triangular plots have areas $36$ m$^2$ and $64$ m$^2$. The shortest side of the larger plot is $12$ m. How long is the corresponding side of the smaller plot, in m?
questions.solution_md: The ratio of areas is $\dfrac{36}{64} = \dfrac{9}{16}$, so the ratio of corresponding sides is $\dfrac{3}{4}$. The side of the smaller plot is $12 \times \dfrac{3}{4} = 9$ m. Option (b) multiplies by the ratio of areas, (c) by $\dfrac{4}{3}$ and (d) subtracts the difference of the square roots, $8 - 6 = 2$, from $12$.

questions.stem_md: A trekking map is drawn to a scale of $1 : 50\,000$. Two camps are $7.2$ cm apart on the map. How far apart are they on the ground, in km?
questions.solution_md: $7.2 \text{ cm}$ on the map stands for $7.2 \times 50000 = 360000$ cm on the ground. Since $1 \text{ km} = 100\,000 \text{ cm}$, the distance is $\dfrac{360000}{100000} = 3.6$ km. The other options are slips of a power of $10$ in the change of units.

questions.stem_md: A model ship is built to the scale $1 : 80$. The real ship has a deck of area $4800$ m$^2$. What is the area of the deck of the model, in m$^2$?
questions.solution_md: Areas change by the square of the scale factor: $\left(\dfrac{1}{80}\right)^2 = \dfrac{1}{6400}$, so the model deck has area $\dfrac{4800}{6400} = 0.75$ m$^2$. Option (d) divides by $80$ only, (a) divides by $80^3$ and (b) by $2 \times 80$.

questions.stem_md: A wax replica of a statue is made at the scale $1 : 20$. The volume of the replica is to the volume of the statue in the ratio
questions.solution_md: Lengths are in the ratio $1 : 20$, areas in $1 : 20^2 = 1 : 400$ and volumes in $1 : 20^3 = 1 : 8000$. Option (a) is the ratio of areas, (b) of lengths, and (c) multiplies $20$ by $3$.

questions.stem_md: The perimeters of two similar triangles are in the ratio $5 : 8$. The smaller triangle has area $50$ cm$^2$. What is the area of the larger triangle, in cm$^2$?
questions.solution_md: Perimeters are in the ratio of corresponding sides, so the sides are in the ratio $5 : 8$ and the areas are in the ratio $\left(\dfrac{8}{5}\right)^2 = \dfrac{64}{25}$. The larger area is $50 \times \dfrac{64}{25} = 128$ cm$^2$. Option (b) multiplies by $\dfrac{8}{5}$ only, (c) by $\left(\dfrac{8}{5}\right)^3$ and (d) adds $8 - 5 = 3$ squared units, $50 + 28$.

questions.stem_md: The altitudes drawn to corresponding sides of two similar triangles measure $6$ cm and $9$ cm. The smaller triangle has area $28$ cm$^2$. What is the area of the larger triangle, in cm$^2$?
questions.solution_md: Corresponding altitudes are in the same ratio as corresponding sides, $6 : 9$. The areas are in the ratio $\left(\dfrac{9}{6}\right)^2 = \dfrac{9}{4}$, so the larger area is $28 \times \dfrac{9}{4} = 63$ cm$^2$. Option (c) uses the ratio $\dfrac{3}{2}$ unsquared, (d) cubes it and (a) adds the difference $9 - 6 = 3$.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A triangle with angles $40^\circ$, $65^\circ$ and $75^\circ$ is similar to a triangle with angles $75^\circ$, $40^\circ$ and $65^\circ$.

**Reason (R):** If two angles of one triangle are equal to two angles of another triangle, the triangles are similar.

options.text_md: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true: the two triangles have the same three angles, only listed in a different order. R is the AA condition, and it is exactly why the triangles are similar, so R explains A.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A rectangle $4$ cm by $6$ cm is similar to a rectangle $6$ cm by $9$ cm.

**Reason (R):** Any two rectangles are similar, because all their angles are right angles.

options.text_md: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true: the angles are all $90^\circ$ and $\dfrac{4}{6} = \dfrac{6}{9} = \dfrac{2}{3}$, so the sides are proportional. R is false: equal angles are not enough for a polygon with more than three sides; a $2$ cm by $3$ cm rectangle and a $2$ cm by $5$ cm rectangle have sides in the ratios $1$ and $\dfrac{3}{5}$.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A triangle with sides $5$ cm, $12$ cm, $13$ cm is similar to a triangle with sides $10$ cm, $24$ cm, $28$ cm.

**Reason (R):** If the three sides of one triangle are proportional to the three sides of another triangle, the two triangles are similar.

options.text_md: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

questions.solution_md: R is true; it is the SSS condition. A is false: $\dfrac{10}{5} = 2$ and $\dfrac{24}{12} = 2$, but $\dfrac{28}{13} \ne 2$, so the sides are not proportional. (The correct third side would be $26$ cm.)

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A line drawn through the mid-point of one side of a triangle, parallel to a second side, bisects the third side.

**Reason (R):** The areas of two similar triangles are in the ratio of the squares of their corresponding sides.

options.text_md: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true: the line cuts the two sides in equal parts, $\dfrac{AD}{DB} = 1$, so $\dfrac{AE}{EC} = 1$ by the Basic Proportionality Theorem. R is also true, but it is about areas and says nothing about a line parallel to a side, so it does not explain A.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** If two similar triangles have sides in the ratio $2 : 3$, their areas are in the ratio $4 : 9$.

**Reason (R):** The ratio of the areas of two similar triangles equals the square of the ratio of their corresponding sides.

options.text_md: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

questions.solution_md: Both statements are true, and R is the rule that gives A: $\left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right)^2 = \dfrac{4}{9}$.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** On a map drawn to the scale $1 : 20\,000$, an area of $1$ cm$^2$ stands for $0.04$ km$^2$.

**Reason (R):** Areas on a map are $k$ times the real areas when the lengths are $k$ times the real lengths.

options.text_md: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true: $1$ cm on the map is $20\,000$ cm $= 0.2$ km, so $1$ cm$^2$ is $0.2 \times 0.2 = 0.04$ km$^2$. R is false: areas are $k^2$ times the real areas, not $k$ times.

questions.stem_md: Two congruent triangles are also similar.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: True. Congruent triangles have equal angles and corresponding sides in the ratio $1 : 1$, so they satisfy the definition of similar triangles with scale factor $1$.

questions.stem_md: A line drawn parallel to one side of a triangle always divides the other two sides into equal parts.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. It divides them in the same ratio, not necessarily equal parts: for $AD = 3$, $DB = 6$, $AE = 2$, $EC = 4$ the ratio is $1 : 2$ on both sides, but $AD \ne DB$.

questions.stem_md: $\triangle ABC$ has $\angle B = 70^\circ$, $AB = 5$ cm and $BC = 7$ cm; $\triangle PQR$ has $\angle Q = 70^\circ$, $PQ = 10$ cm and $QR = 14$ cm. These triangles are similar.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: True. $\dfrac{AB}{PQ} = \dfrac{5}{10} = \dfrac{1}{2}$ and $\dfrac{BC}{QR} = \dfrac{7}{14} = \dfrac{1}{2}$, and the included angles are equal, so the SAS condition holds.

questions.stem_md: A rhombus of side $6$ cm with one angle $60^\circ$ and a square of side $12$ cm are similar, because their corresponding sides are in the ratio $1 : 2$.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. Proportional sides are not enough for polygons with four or more sides: the angles of the rhombus are $60^\circ$ and $120^\circ$, those of the square are all $90^\circ$, so the corresponding angles are not equal.

questions.stem_md: A scale model is built at $1 : 10$. Its volume is $\dfrac{1}{1000}$ of the volume of the real object.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: True. Volumes change by the cube of the scale factor: $\left(\dfrac{1}{10}\right)^3 = \dfrac{1}{1000}$.

questions.stem_md: Triangles with sides $3$, $4$, $5$ and $6$, $8$, $11$ (all in cm) are similar.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. $\dfrac{6}{3} = 2$ and $\dfrac{8}{4} = 2$ but $\dfrac{11}{5} = 2.2$, so the three pairs of sides are not proportional.

questions.stem_md: If $\triangle ABC \sim \triangle XYZ$ and $\angle B = 53^\circ$, then $\angle Y$ = ___ degrees.
questions.solution_md: Corresponding angles of similar triangles are equal, and $B$ corresponds to $Y$, so $\angle Y = 53^\circ$.

questions.stem_md: The areas of two similar triangles are in the ratio $25 : 81$, so their corresponding sides are in the ratio $5 :$ ___.
questions.solution_md: The ratio of sides is the square root of the ratio of areas: $\sqrt{25} : \sqrt{81} = 5 : 9$.

questions.stem_md: On a map of scale $1 : 25\,000$, a stretch of canal $1$ cm long represents ___ km on the ground.
In a triangle $ABC$ with $DE \parallel BC$ ($D$ on $AB$, $E$ on $AC$), $AD = 5$ cm and $AB = 8$ cm. Then $\dfrac{AE}{AC}$ = ___.
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{AE}{AC} = \dfrac{AD}{AB} = \dfrac{5}{8}$, that is $0.625$.

questions.stem_md: A model of a bridge is made at the scale $1 : 5$. Its volume is $1 :$ ___ of the real bridge's volume.
questions.solution_md: Volumes are in the ratio of the cubes of the lengths: $5^3 = 125$, so the ratio is $1 : 125$.

questions.stem_md: The areas of two similar triangles are in the ratio $49 : 100$. Their perimeters are therefore in the ratio $7 :$ ___.
questions.solution_md: The perimeters are in the ratio of the corresponding sides, which is $\sqrt{49} : \sqrt{100} = 7 : 10$.

questions.stem_md: $\triangle ABC \sim \triangle DEF$ with $AB = 7.5$ cm, $DE = 10$ cm and $BC = 9$ cm. Find $EF$, in cm.
questions.solution_md: $AB$ and $BC$ correspond to $DE$ and $EF$. With $EF = x$ cm: $\dfrac{7.5}{10} = \dfrac{9}{x} \Rightarrow x = \dfrac{9 \times 10}{7.5} = 12$.

questions.stem_md: A flat roof is a triangle $ABC$. A beam $DE$ parallel to $BC$ is fixed with $AD : DB = 3 : 5$ and $AE = 4.5$ m. Find $AC$, in m.
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{AE}{EC} = \dfrac{AD}{DB} = \dfrac{3}{5}$, so $EC = \dfrac{5 \times 4.5}{3} = 7.5$ m and $AC = AE + EC = 4.5 + 7.5 = 12$ m.

questions.stem_md: In a triangle, a line parallel to the third side divides the other two sides so that the parts, in cm, are $x$ and $x - 2$ on one side and $x + 2$ and $x - 1$ on the other (in the same order). Find $x$.
questions.solution_md: The parts are in proportion: $\dfrac{x}{x - 2} = \dfrac{x + 2}{x - 1}$, so $x(x - 1) = (x - 2)(x + 2) \Rightarrow x^2 - x = x^2 - 4 \Rightarrow x = 4$. Check: $\dfrac{4}{2} = \dfrac{6}{3}$.

questions.stem_md: Two similar triangular lawns have areas $54$ m$^2$ and $96$ m$^2$. The longest side of the smaller lawn is $9$ m. Find the longest side of the larger lawn, in m.
questions.solution_md: The ratio of areas is $\dfrac{54}{96} = \dfrac{9}{16}$, so the ratio of sides is $\dfrac{3}{4}$, and the larger side is $9 \times \dfrac{4}{3} = 12$ m.

questions.stem_md: On a district map drawn to the scale $1 : 200\,000$, two bus stops are $5.5$ cm apart. How far apart are they in reality, in km?
A model aeroplane has a wingspan of $24$ cm; the real wingspan is $36$ m. The real fuselage is $45$ m long. How long is the model fuselage, in cm?
questions.solution_md: Scale: $24 \text{ cm} : 36 \text{ m} = 24 : 3600 = 1 : 150$. The model fuselage is $\dfrac{4500}{150} = 30$ cm, as the real length is $4500$ cm.

questions.stem_md: A scale model of a water tank at $1 : 20$ holds $250$ cm$^3$ when full. How many cubic metres does the real tank hold?
questions.solution_md: The real volume is $20^3 = 8000$ times the model's: $250 \times 8000 = 2\,000\,000$ cm$^3$. Since $1 \text{ m}^3 = 1\,000\,000 \text{ cm}^3$, the tank holds $\dfrac{2000000}{1000000} = 2$ m$^3$.

questions.stem_md: A triangular banner $ABC$ has area $125$ cm$^2$. A stitch line $DE \parallel BC$ is sewn with $AD : DB = 2 : 3$. Find the area of the small triangle $ADE$, in cm$^2$.
questions.solution_md: $\triangle ADE \sim \triangle ABC$ with $\dfrac{AD}{AB} = \dfrac{2}{2 + 3} = \dfrac{2}{5}$. The areas are in the ratio $\dfrac{4}{25}$, so area $= \dfrac{4}{25} \times 125 = 20$ cm$^2$.

questions.stem_md: A carpenter cuts two triangular braces. One has sides $9$ cm, $12$ cm and $15$ cm, the other $15$ cm, $20$ cm and $25$ cm. Show that the braces are similar and write the scale factor from the smaller to the larger.

answer.model_answer_md:
Ratios of corresponding sides, shortest to shortest and so on: $\dfrac{9}{15} = \dfrac{3}{5}$, $\dfrac{12}{20} = \dfrac{3}{5}$, $\dfrac{15}{25} = \dfrac{3}{5}$.

The three ratios are equal, so the triangles are similar by the SSS condition, and the scale factor from the smaller to the larger is $\dfrac{5}{3}$.

questions.solution_md: Divide each side of the smaller brace by the corresponding side of the larger; equal ratios mean SSS similarity.

questions.stem_md: The diagonals $AC$ and $BD$ of trapezium $ABCD$, in which $AB \parallel DC$, meet at $O$. Name a pair of similar triangles, give the condition that makes them similar, and write the proportion of their sides.

answer.model_answer_md:
$\triangle AOB \sim \triangle COD$. $\angle AOB = \angle COD$ (vertically opposite angles) and $\angle OAB = \angle OCD$ (alternate angles, $AB \parallel DC$), so the triangles are similar by the AA condition.

Corresponding sides are proportional: $\dfrac{AO}{CO} = \dfrac{BO}{DO} = \dfrac{AB}{CD}$.

questions.solution_md: Vertically opposite angles and alternate angles give two equal pairs of angles.

questions.stem_md: A town map is drawn to the scale $1 : 60\,000$. The road from the mill to the ferry measures $4.5$ cm on the map. Find its real length in kilometres.
questions.solution_md: Multiply the map length by the scale denominator, then change centimetres to kilometres.

questions.stem_md: Two similar triangular gardens have areas $25$ m$^2$ and $49$ m$^2$. The smaller garden has a boundary of $30$ m. Find the boundary of the larger garden.

answer.model_answer_md:
The ratio of corresponding sides is the square root of the ratio of areas: $\sqrt{25} : \sqrt{49} = 5 : 7$.

Perimeters are in the same ratio as sides, so the larger perimeter is $30 \times \dfrac{7}{5} = 42$ m.

questions.solution_md: Sides, and so perimeters, are in the square root of the ratio of areas.

questions.stem_md: A segment $ST$ is drawn parallel to side $QR$ of $\triangle PQR$, with $S$ on $PQ$ and $T$ on $PR$. Given $PS = 3.6$ cm, $SQ = 2.4$ cm and $PT = 4.5$ cm, find $TR$.

answer.model_answer_md:
By the Basic Proportionality Theorem, $\dfrac{PS}{SQ} = \dfrac{PT}{TR}$.

$TR = \dfrac{PT \times SQ}{PS} = \dfrac{4.5 \times 2.4}{3.6} = 3$ cm.

questions.solution_md: Apply the Basic Proportionality Theorem with the parallel segment $ST$.

questions.stem_md: $\triangle ABC$ has $\angle B = 72^\circ$, $AB = 8$ cm and $BC = 10$ cm. $\triangle PQR$ has $\angle Q = 72^\circ$, $PQ = 12$ cm and $QR = 15$ cm. Show that the triangles are similar, and find $AC$ if $PR = 21$ cm.

answer.model_answer_md:
$\dfrac{AB}{PQ} = \dfrac{8}{12} = \dfrac{2}{3}$ and $\dfrac{BC}{QR} = \dfrac{10}{15} = \dfrac{2}{3}$, and the included angles $\angle B = \angle Q = 72^\circ$.

The sides including the equal angle are proportional, so $\triangle ABC \sim \triangle PQR$ by the SAS condition.

$\dfrac{AC}{PR} = \dfrac{2}{3}$, so $AC = 21 \times \dfrac{2}{3} = 14$ cm.

questions.solution_md: Check that the sides around the equal angles are proportional; the third sides then have the same ratio.

questions.stem_md: A rafter $DE$ is parallel to the tie-beam $BC$ of a triangular truss $ABC$, with $D$ on $AB$ and $E$ on $AC$. $AB = 12$ cm, $AD = 4.8$ cm and $AE = 3.6$ cm in the scale drawing. Find $AC$ and $EC$.

answer.model_answer_md:
$\triangle ADE \sim \triangle ABC$, so $\dfrac{AE}{AC} = \dfrac{AD}{AB} = \dfrac{4.8}{12} = 0.4$.

$AC = \dfrac{AE}{0.4} = \dfrac{3.6}{0.4} = 9$ cm.

$EC = AC - AE = 9 - 3.6 = 5.4$ cm.

questions.solution_md: The parallel line cuts the sides in the same proportion, so $\dfrac{AE}{AC}$ equals $\dfrac{AD}{AB}$.

questions.stem_md: $EFGH$ is a trapezium with $EF \parallel HG$, $EF = 14$ cm and $HG = 10$ cm. Its diagonals $EG$ and $FH$ cut at $K$, and $EK = 8.4$ cm. Find $KG$ and the ratio of the areas of $\triangle EKF$ and $\triangle GKH$.

answer.model_answer_md:
$\triangle EKF \sim \triangle GKH$ (AA), so $\dfrac{EK}{KG} = \dfrac{EF}{HG} = \dfrac{14}{10}$.

$KG = \dfrac{8.4 \times 10}{14} = 6$ cm.

The areas of similar triangles are in the ratio of the squares of corresponding sides: $\dfrac{\text{area } EKF}{\text{area } GKH} = \left(\dfrac{14}{10}\right)^2 = \dfrac{49}{25}$, that is $49 : 25$.

questions.solution_md: The diagonals of a trapezium cut each other in the ratio of the parallel sides; areas go as the square of that ratio.

questions.stem_md: An architect builds a model of a hospital block at the scale $1 : 75$. The real block is $33$ m high and has a floor area of $900$ m$^2$. Find the height of the model in cm and the floor area of the model in cm$^2$.

answer.model_answer_md:
Height: $33 \text{ m} = 3300$ cm, so the model height is $\dfrac{3300}{75} = 44$ cm.

Areas change by the square of the scale factor: $75^2 = 5625$.

Real area $= 900 \text{ m}^2 = 9\,000\,000 \text{ cm}^2$, so the model area is $\dfrac{9000000}{5625} = 1600$ cm$^2$.

questions.solution_md: Lengths are divided by $75$ and areas by $75^2$.

questions.stem_md: In right-angled $\triangle PQR$ the right angle is at $Q$, $PQ = 6$ cm and $QR = 8$ cm. The perpendicular from $Q$ meets the hypotenuse $PR$ at $S$. Prove that $\triangle PSQ \sim \triangle PQR$ and find $PS$.

answer.model_answer_md:
In $\triangle PSQ$ and $\triangle PQR$: $\angle P$ is common and $\angle PSQ = \angle PQR = 90^\circ$. By the AA condition $\triangle PSQ \sim \triangle PQR$.

$PR^2 = 6^2 + 8^2 = 100$, so $PR = 10$ cm.

$\dfrac{PS}{PQ} = \dfrac{PQ}{PR}$, so $PS = \dfrac{PQ^2}{PR} = \dfrac{6 \times 6}{10} = 3.6$ cm.

questions.solution_md: A common angle and two right angles prove similarity; then equate corresponding ratios.

marking_scheme.step: AA: common angle P and right angles

questions.stem_md: A girl $1.5$ m tall casts a shadow $2$ m long on level ground. At the same time a flagpole casts a shadow $14$ m long. Find the height of the flagpole and the distance from its top to the tip of its shadow.

answer.model_answer_md:
The sun's rays are parallel and the girl and the pole are both vertical, so the two right triangles are similar (AA).

Height of the pole: $\dfrac{h}{14} = \dfrac{1.5}{2}$, so $h = \dfrac{1.5}{2} \times 14 = 10.5$ m.

Distance from the top to the tip: $\sqrt{10.5^2 + 14^2}$: $10.5^2 + 14^2 = 306.25$, so the distance is $\sqrt{306.25} = 17.5$ m.

questions.solution_md: Parallel rays and vertical objects give equal angles; compare height to shadow, then use Pythagoras.

questions.stem_md:
In $\triangle ABC$, $AB = 14$ cm, $AC = 10$ cm and $BC = 12$ cm. The point $P$ lies on $AB$ with $AP = 4$ cm, and $Q$ lies on $AC$ so that $\angle APQ = \angle ACB$.

(i) Prove that $\triangle APQ \sim \triangle ACB$.

(ii) Find $AQ$.

(iii) Find $PQ$.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) In $\triangle APQ$ and $\triangle ACB$: $\angle A$ is common and $\angle APQ = \angle ACB$ (given). By the AA condition, $\triangle APQ \sim \triangle ACB$, with $P \to C$, $Q \to B$.

(ii) $\dfrac{AP}{AC} = \dfrac{AQ}{AB}$, so with $AQ = x$ cm: $\dfrac{4}{10} = \dfrac{x}{14} \Rightarrow x = \dfrac{4 \times 14}{10} = 5.6$.

(iii) $\dfrac{PQ}{CB} = \dfrac{AP}{AC}$, so $PQ = \dfrac{4 \times 12}{10} = 4.8$ cm.

questions.solution_md: The triangles share angle $A$ and have one more pair of equal angles; match $P$ with $C$ and $Q$ with $B$.

questions.stem_md: $DE \parallel BC$ in $\triangle ABC$, with $D$ on $AB$ and $E$ on $AC$. $AD = x + 4$, $DB = x + 1$, $AE = 2x - 4$ and $EC = x - 1$ (all in cm). Find $x$, and hence the lengths $AB$ and $AC$.

answer.model_answer_md:
By the Basic Proportionality Theorem, $\dfrac{AD}{DB} = \dfrac{AE}{EC}$: $\dfrac{x + 4}{x + 1} = \dfrac{2x - 4}{x - 1}$.

$(x + 4)(x - 1) = (x + 1)(2x - 4) \Rightarrow x^2 + 3x - 4 = 2x^2 - 2x - 4 \Rightarrow x^2 - 5x = 0 \Rightarrow x = 5 \text{ or } x = 0$.

$x = 0$ is rejected, since then $EC = -1$. So $x = 5$.

$AD = 9$, $DB = 6$, so $AB = 15$ cm; $AE = 6$, $EC = 4$, so $AC = 10$ cm. Check: $\dfrac{9}{6} = \dfrac{6}{4}$.

questions.solution_md: Equate the two ratios, expand to a quadratic, reject the root that gives a negative length.

questions.stem_md:
$\triangle ABC \sim \triangle DEF$ and their areas are $81$ cm$^2$ and $144$ cm$^2$. The perimeter of $\triangle ABC$ is $36$ cm, and the altitude of $\triangle DEF$ on $EF$ is $10.4$ cm.

(i) Find the ratio $AB : DE$.

(ii) Find the perimeter of $\triangle DEF$.

(iii) Find the altitude of $\triangle ABC$ on $BC$.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) The ratio of areas is $\dfrac{81}{144} = \dfrac{9}{16}$, so $AB : DE = \sqrt{9} : \sqrt{16} = 3 : 4$.

(ii) Perimeters are in the ratio of corresponding sides: $36 \times \dfrac{4}{3} = 48$ cm.

(iii) Corresponding altitudes are in the same ratio $3 : 4$: $10.4 \times \dfrac{3}{4} = 7.8$ cm.

questions.solution_md: Take the square root of the area ratio; perimeters and altitudes share the ratio of the sides.

questions.stem_md:
A triangular plot $ABC$ of area $200$ m$^2$ is divided by a fence $DE$ parallel to $BC$, with $D$ on $AB$, $E$ on $AC$ and $AD : DB = 2 : 3$.

(i) Find $AD : AB$.

(ii) Find the area of the part $ADE$.

(iii) Find the area of the part $DBCE$.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) $\dfrac{AD}{AB} = \dfrac{2}{2 + 3} = \dfrac{2}{5}$.

(ii) $\triangle ADE \sim \triangle ABC$, so the areas are in the ratio $\left(\dfrac{2}{5}\right)^2 = \dfrac{4}{25}$: area $ADE = \left(\dfrac{2}{5}\right)^2 \times 200 = 32$ m$^2$.

(iii) Area $DBCE = 200 - 32 = 168$ m$^2$.

questions.solution_md: The small triangle is similar to the whole one, so its area is the square of the side ratio times the whole area.

questions.stem_md:
A map of a nature reserve is drawn to the scale $1 : 40\,000$.

(i) A footpath measures $9$ cm on the map. How long is it in km?

(ii) A lake covers $6.5$ cm$^2$ on the map. Find its real area in km$^2$.

(iii) A fence $14$ km long is to be drawn on the map. How many cm long will it be?

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) $9 \times 40\,000 = 360\,000$ cm, that is $\dfrac{360000}{100000} = 3.6$ km.

(ii) $1$ cm on the map is $0.4$ km, so $1$ cm$^2$ is $0.4 \times 0.4 = 0.16$ km$^2$; the lake covers $6.5 \times 0.16 = 1.04$ km$^2$.

(iii) $14 \text{ km} = 1\,400\,000$ cm, so the map length is $\dfrac{1400000}{40000} = 35$ cm.

questions.solution_md: Lengths are multiplied by $40\,000$ and areas by $40\,000^2$; going back to the map divides.

questions.stem_md:
A sculptor makes a model of a fountain at the scale $1 : 10$. The real fountain is $3.5$ m high, has a stone surface of $24$ m$^2$ and holds $6.4$ m$^3$ of water.

(i) How high is the model, in cm?

(ii) What stone surface does the model have, in cm$^2$?

(iii) How much water does the model hold, in cm$^3$?
questions.solution_md: Divide lengths by $10$, areas by $100$ and volumes by $1000$, then change units.

questions.stem_md:
In $\triangle ABC$, $D$ is on $AB$ and $E$ is on $AC$ with $DE \parallel BC$. $AD = 6$ cm, $DB = 9$ cm, $AE = 8$ cm, $BC = 25$ cm and the area of $\triangle ABC$ is $150$ cm$^2$. Show all working.

(a) Find $EC$ and $AC$.

(b) Find the ratio $DE : BC$ and the length of $DE$.

(c) Find the area of $\triangle ADE$ and the area of the trapezium $DBCE$.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** By the Basic Proportionality Theorem $\dfrac{AD}{DB} = \dfrac{AE}{EC}$, so $EC = \dfrac{8 \times 9}{6} = 12$ cm. Then $AC = AE + EC$: $8 + 12 = 20$ cm.

**(b)** $\triangle ADE \sim \triangle ABC$ (AA: common angle $A$, and $\angle ADE = \angle ABC$ because $DE \parallel BC$). So $\dfrac{DE}{BC} = \dfrac{AD}{AB} = \dfrac{6}{6 + 9} = \dfrac{2}{5}$, that is $DE : BC = 2 : 5$, and $DE = 25 \times \dfrac{2}{5} = 10$ cm.

**(c)** The areas are in the ratio of the squares of corresponding sides: $\left(\dfrac{2}{5}\right)^2 = \dfrac{4}{25}$. Area of $\triangle ADE = \dfrac{4}{25} \times 150 = 24$ cm$^2$. Area of trapezium $DBCE = 150 - 24 = 126$ cm$^2$.

questions.solution_md: Basic Proportionality Theorem for EC; similar triangles ADE and ABC for the ratio of DE to BC; area ratio is the square of the side ratio; the trapezium is the whole minus the small triangle.

marking_scheme.step: (c) area ratio 4 : 25 and area ADE = 24 cm^2

questions.stem_md:
$ABCD$ is a trapezium with $AB \parallel DC$, $AB = 18$ cm, $DC = 12$ cm and $AC = 25$ cm. The diagonals meet at $O$, and the area of $\triangle AOB$ is $81$ cm$^2$. Show all working.

(a) Name a pair of similar triangles with the reason, and find $AO$ and $OC$.

(b) Find the area of $\triangle COD$.

(c) Find the areas of $\triangle AOD$ and $\triangle BOC$, and of the trapezium $ABCD$.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** In $\triangle AOB$ and $\triangle COD$: $\angle AOB = \angle COD$ (vertically opposite) and $\angle OAB = \angle OCD$ (alternate angles, $AB \parallel DC$), so $\triangle AOB \sim \triangle COD$ (AA). Then $\dfrac{AO}{OC} = \dfrac{AB}{DC} = \dfrac{18}{12} = \dfrac{3}{2}$, so $AO = 25 \times \dfrac{3}{5} = 15$ cm and $OC = 25 - 15 = 10$ cm.

**(b)** The areas are in the ratio $\left(\dfrac{3}{2}\right)^2 = \dfrac{9}{4}$, so area $COD = 81 \times \dfrac{4}{9} = 36$ cm$^2$.

**(c)** $\triangle AOD$ and $\triangle AOB$ have the same height from $A$ to $BD$, so their areas are in the ratio of the bases $OD : OB = 2 : 3$: area $AOD = 81 \times \dfrac{2}{3} = 54$ cm$^2$. $\triangle ADC$ and $\triangle BDC$ stand on $DC$ between the same parallels, so they have equal areas; removing $\triangle DOC$ from both gives area $BOC = 54$ cm$^2$. The trapezium has area $81 + 36 + 54 + 54 = 225$ cm$^2$.

questions.solution_md: AA similarity of triangles AOB and COD; the diagonals divide each other in the ratio AB : DC; areas of similar triangles go as the square of the ratio of sides; triangles with a common height have areas in the ratio of their bases.

questions.stem_md:
A man $1.6$ m tall stands beside a tower. In the same sunlight his shadow is $1.2$ m long and the tower's shadow is $21$ m long. Show all working.

(a) Explain why the two right-angled triangles formed are similar, and find the height of the tower.

(b) Find the distance from the top of the tower to the tip of its shadow.

(c) Find the scale factor from the man's triangle to the tower's triangle, the ratio of their areas, and verify it by finding both areas.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** The sun's rays are parallel, so the angle of elevation is the same for both; each triangle has a right angle at the foot of the vertical object. By the AA condition the triangles are similar. The scale factor is $\dfrac{21}{1.2} = 17.5$, so the tower is $1.6 \times 17.5 = 28$ m high.

**(b)** $PR^2 = 28^2 + 21^2$: $28^2 + 21^2 = 1225$, so $PR = \sqrt{1225} = 35$ m.

**(c)** The scale factor is $17.5$, so the ratio of the areas is $17.5^2$: $17.5 \times 17.5 = 306.25$. Area of the tower's triangle $= \dfrac{1}{2} \times 21 \times 28 = 294$ m$^2$ and area of the man's triangle $= \dfrac{1}{2} \times 1.2 \times 1.6 = 0.96$ m$^2$; and $\dfrac{294}{0.96} = 306.25$, which agrees.

questions.solution_md: AA similarity from parallel rays and vertical objects; scale factor from the shadows; Pythagoras for the slant distance; areas of similar triangles go as the square of the scale factor.

questions.stem_md:
In right-angled $\triangle ABC$ the right angle is at $B$, $AB = 15$ cm, $BC = 20$ cm and $AC = 25$ cm. $BD$ is drawn perpendicular to $AC$, with $D$ on $AC$. Show all working.

(a) Show that $\triangle ABD \sim \triangle ACB$ and find $AD$.

(b) Find $DC$ and $BD$.

(c) Find the areas of $\triangle ABD$ and $\triangle BDC$, and show that their ratio is the square of $AB : BC$.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** In $\triangle ABD$ and $\triangle ACB$: $\angle A$ is common and $\angle ADB = \angle ABC = 90^\circ$, so $\triangle ABD \sim \triangle ACB$ (AA). Hence $\dfrac{AD}{AB} = \dfrac{AB}{AC}$ and $AD = \dfrac{15 \times 15}{25} = 9$ cm.

**(b)** In the same way $\triangle CBD \sim \triangle CAB$, so $DC = \dfrac{BC^2}{AC} = \dfrac{20 \times 20}{25} = 16$ cm; check: $9 + 16 = 25$. Also $BD = \dfrac{AB \times BC}{AC} = \dfrac{15 \times 20}{25} = 12$ cm.

**(c)** Area $ABD = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 9 \times 12 = 54$ cm$^2$ and area $BDC = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 12 \times 16 = 96$ cm$^2$. Their ratio is $\dfrac{54}{96} = \dfrac{9}{16}$, and $\left(\dfrac{AB}{BC}\right)^2$: $\left(\dfrac{15}{20}\right)^2 = \dfrac{9}{16}$, which is the same, since $\triangle ABD \sim \triangle BDC$ with ratio $AB : BC$.

questions.solution_md: AA similarity from the shared angle and the right angles; corresponding ratios give AD, DC and BD; the two small triangles are similar to each other, so their areas go as the square of AB : BC.
